title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarking & Runbooks
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview:

This document is the canonical reference for the Redwood Serving Runtime: end-to-end runtime architecture, kernel scheduling and placement policies, step-by-step profiling and performance playbooks, the benchmarking suite and results, recent release notes, known issues and operational runbooks, and pointers to the team wiki. It is intended for engineers (runtime, infra, SRE), oncall responders, and platform owners who operate or optimize inference at production scale.

Goals:
- Describe the architecture and service boundaries for the serving runtime.
- Document kernel scheduling policies and rationale for placement decisions.
- Provide a reproducible profiling and perf investigation playbook.
- Record benchmarking methodology and representative results for common workloads.
- Maintain runbooks for incidents and operational tasks.
- Track recent release notes and outstanding known issues.

1) Runtime Architecture (high level):

Summary:
The serving runtime is a microservices-based inference stack optimized for high-throughput, low-latency LLM inference. Core logical components: request router (redwood-router), model manager (model-dispatcher), execution engine (inference-worker), KV cache service (kv-cache), and metrics/tracing (rt-observability). The control plane (control-api) handles model lifecycle, rollouts, and placement rules.

Key service names and responsibilities:
- redwood-router: HTTP/GRPC edge that performs authentication, routing policies (latency/cost/region), and initial request shaping.
- model-dispatcher: maps requests to model variants and execution pools; enforces canary/A-B rollouts and quota checks.
- inference-worker: GPU/CPU process that runs model kernels (supports quantized kernels, mixed-precision) and exposes a local gRPC inference API.
- kv-cache: in-memory KV cache for prefix/KV caching and fast resume. Integrated with inference-worker for low-latency cache hits.
- control-api: administrative plane for deployments, model pinning, and autoscale policies.
- rt-observability: collects token-level latency, GPU metrics, cache-hit rates, and writes to Prom/Tempo for dashboards.

Deployment topology:
- Edge layer in each region runs redwood-router instances (k8s pods behind LB).
- Dedicated inference pools are grouped by model family + quantization profile + GPU type (e.g., llama-3-70b-q4_nh4-A100-80GB-pool).
- Autoscaler autoscale-controller uses request rate and target P99 latency to adjust replica counts with a safety floor.

SLOs and targets (operational):
- P95 response latency (1k tokens): <= 300ms for hosted low-latency tier.
- P99 response latency (1k tokens): <= 700ms for hosted low-latency tier.
- Availability: 99.95% per region for production pools.
- Cache hit rate target: >= 20% for high-reuse workloads (prefix-heavy).

2) Kernel Scheduling & Placement Policy:

Objectives:
- Minimize tail latency by avoiding noisy neighbors and contention for GPU resources.
- Maximize throughput by grouping compatible batch-size distributions together.

Scheduling rules (high-level):
1. Model family affinity: prefer scheduling requests for the same model variant on dedicated pools to reuse JIT/compiled kernels and KV cache.
2. Sequence length bucketing: group by common sequence-length distribution to choose the right kernel and reduce memory overcommit.
3. Quantization/precision isolation: separate INT8/FP16 workloads to avoid kernel selection variability.
4. Noise isolation: use machine-labels and topology-aware placement to avoid mixing noisy background workloads with latency-critical inference.
5. Fallback policy: when dedicated pool capacity is exhausted, route to compatible lower-cost pool only if the request's latency SLO allows (controlled in redwood-router routing policy).

Kernel selection logic (runtime):
- inference-worker maintains a small kernel catalog per model variant keyed by (model-arch, seq-length-range, batch-size-range, precision).
- On first warmup, the worker runs microbenchmarks for the prominent seq-lengths to pick preferred kernels and stores the decision in local cache and control plane.
- Periodic re-evaluation occurs during low-traffic windows or following kernel library updates.

3) Profiling Playbook (step-by-step):

When investigating performance regressions or unexpected latency: numbered steps to reproduce and triage
1) Gather context: request IDs, route, model variant, exact input sequence lengths, and timeframe.
2) Pull observability traces: P99 traces from rt-observability and Tempo for the time window.
3) Identify latency stage: edge (auth/routing), model-dispatch, network (grpc), kernel execution, or post-processing.
4) For kernel-level investigation: enable detailed GPU profiling with our instrumented perf-sidecar on a single replica. Run:
   - docker exec -it perf-sidecar /usr/local/bin/run_gpu_profile.sh --target-pid <worker-pid> --duration 60s --out /tmp/profile.tar.gz
5) Reproduce workload on staging: use perf-runner with the captured request set:
   - ./perf-runner --requests requests.json --model llama-3-70b --pool staging-70b-a100 --concurrency 8 --capture-traces
6) Inspect kernel timelines and NVTX spans (timeline in /tmp/profile.tar.gz). Confirm KV cache hit rates and memory usage.
7) If kernel contention is observed: consider immediate mitigation: reduce concurrency on pool (scale down), or migrate a noisy tenant to a separate pool.
8) Open an incident with evidence and recommended remediation (see Runbooks).

Recommended profiling flags and thresholds:
- Enable nvprof/Nsight for 60s with sample frequency = 100ms.
- Flag a regression if median per-token kernel time increases > 20% or P99 increases > 30% compared to baseline.

4) Benchmarking Suite (methodology and example results):

Bench methodology:
- Benchmarks are run with perf-bench v2.0 on representative request traces and synthetic workloads. Each benchmark records throughput (tokens/s), latency distribution (P50/P95/P99), GPU utilization, and memory high-water mark.
- Use standardized configs for model variants and hardware families. Run 3 independent trials and report median.

Representative table (example):
| Model Variant | HW | Batch | Workload | Tokens/s | P95 Latency | Notes |
|---------------|----|-------|----------|----------:|------------:|-------|
| llama-3-70b-q4 | A100-80GB | dynamic | chat-avg (512) | 18,200 | 280ms | q4 optimized kernels, prefix cache ON |
| llama-3-13b-fp16 | A100-40GB | 8 | assistant-long (1024) | 24,900 | 220ms | fp16 kernels, batch 8 sweet spot |

Benchmark reproducibility (commands):
- ./perf-bench --model <model> --hw a100-80 --trace sample-trace.json --warmup 300 --duration 1200 --out results.json

5) Release Notes (selected recent entries):
- 2026-11-15: inference-worker v2.8.0: added adaptive kernel selection for seq-length < 256; reduced warmup overhead by 18%; fixed mem leak in attention buffer.
- 2026-09-03: kv-cache v1.4.2: improved prefix eviction policy and added metrics for per-tenant cache hit-rate.
- 2026-06-21: redwood-router v1.12.0: routing policy rule engine supports cost-based routing and model fallback chaining.

Upgrade guidance:
1. Schedule kernel library updates during low-traffic maintenance windows.
2. Validate with perf-bench against a sampled production trace.
3. Use canary rollout with 5% traffic and monitor token-level P95/P99 for 2 hours.

6) Known Issues (operational, with workarounds):
- ISSUE-2026-047: Occasional P99 spikes when mixed batch-size workloads co-locate on A100-80GB pools. Workaround: apply scheduling label "avoid-mixed-batches" to the pool or set pod anti-affinity for heterogeneous batch patterns.
- ISSUE-2026-032: KV cache hot-eviction for very long prefix session (>= 50k tokens) causing unexpected cold starts. Workaround: enable session-sticky pool assignment for long-running sessions and increase kv-cache memory limit for those pools.
- ISSUE-2026-019: Some INT8 kernels fall back to slower FP16 path on older drivers. Workaround: pin drivers to 525.85 and use image tag redwood/inference-worker:stable-2026-06.

7) Runtime Runbooks (operational procedures):
A) Immediate P99 latency storm (oncall):
1. Acknowledge page and post initial status on #oncall-runtime.
2. Run /contrib/diagnostics/collect_realtime_snapshot.sh --window 10m --out /tmp/snap.tgz and upload to incident.
3. Check rt-observability dashboards: model-level P99, kernel-level spans, GPU util, and queue lengths.
4. If kernel contention: scale pool replicas by +25% and set temporary max_concurrency per replica to reduce queuing.
5. If external router throttling: confirm redwood-router logs for 429/503 and adjust rate-limits or route to fallback pool.
6. After mitigation, create a postmortem and attach profiling artifacts.

B) Failed canary for kernel update:
1. Abort rollout in control-api and rollback to previous image tag.
2. Mark the release as blocked and notify release owner and release-manager.
3. Run benchmark suite to reproduce regression locally and open a PR with root cause analysis.

Appendix: Useful commands and configs:
- Show pool status: kubectl -n inference get pods -l app=inference-worker -o wide
- Dump model-dispatcher routes: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://control-api.internal/v1/routes | jq .
- Example pool config (YAML):
  name: llama-3-70b-q4-a100-pool
  labels: ["model:llama-3-70b","precision:q4","batching:dynamic"]
  min_replicas: 2
  max_replicas: 50
  concurrency_per_replica: 12

Documentation maintenance rules:
- Major architecture changes require an ADR and an updated section here.
- Profiling/playbook changes should include sample commands and a reproducible bench.

If you identify missing content or need a follow-up deep dive (e.g., kernel internals for a specific model family), open a ticket assigned to runtime-architecture backlog and tag reviewers listed above.
